text: When you have had a demanding day, what restores you most reliably?

options.text: Talking through the day with someone I trust.
Being alone long enough to hear my own thoughts.
Doing something active with other people.
Going somewhere quiet and mentally switching off.

text: When a new idea occurs to you, what happens first?

options.text: I want to say it out loud and see where it goes.
I turn it over privately before sharing it.
I immediately look for people or situations where I can try it.
I keep it inside until it feels fully formed.

text: At a gathering where you know few people, you are more likely to:

options.text: Start a conversation simply to see what develops.
Wait until there is a natural reason to speak.
Move between different people and groups.
Find one person or a quiet corner that feels comfortable.

text: After making an important decision, you prefer to:

options.text: Talk about it and hear reactions.
Sit with it privately and make sure it feels settled inside.
Explain your reasoning to someone else.
Keep the decision mostly to yourself until you have processed it.

text: When you are learning something difficult, you tend to:

options.text: Ask questions as they arise.
Think through the questions before asking them.
Learn by discussing the topic with others.
Learn best through concentrated independent study.

text: If you suddenly have an entirely free evening, your instinct is to:

options.text: See whether someone wants to do something.
Protect the evening for myself.
Look for something happening outside the house.
Enjoy having no social obligation at all.

text: When a problem is emotionally complicated, you often:

options.text: Need to talk it through to understand it.
Need time alone before you can explain it.
Discover what you think while speaking.
Discover what you think while reflecting.

text: When you enter a new environment, your attention naturally goes toward:

options.text: What people are doing and how the atmosphere is moving.
How the place affects you personally.
Who might be interesting to meet.
What you notice internally before engaging.

text: When you disagree with someone, your first impulse is often to:

options.text: Engage them and work it out aloud.
Step back and formulate your position.
Keep the conversation going until something useful emerges.
Pause because you need space to know what you really think.

text: Which feels more natural when you have a thought you are excited about?

options.text: Sharing it while it is still developing.
Protecting it until I know what I mean.
Building on it through conversation.
Exploring it privately before anyone else influences it.

text: When you remember an experience, what tends to stand out?

options.text: The specific things that happened.
The meaning the experience has acquired over time.
Concrete details, sensations, and what was actually said.
The pattern or lesson I think was underneath it.

text: When someone gives you instructions, you prefer:

options.text: Clear steps and concrete expectations.
The overall purpose so I can decide how to approach it.
Examples of exactly what the finished result should look like.
Freedom to interpret the underlying idea.

text: When solving a practical problem, you trust most:

options.text: What has worked before.
What the situation might become if I change the approach.
Observable evidence.
A pattern I notice that suggests a new solution.

text: Which statement sounds more like you?

options.text: Details often tell me what I need to know.
Details are useful, but the larger pattern matters more.
I notice what is tangible before speculating.
I often notice implications before I can explain the details.

text: When reading a story, you are more drawn to:

options.text: What actually happened and how the characters behaved.
What the story could be saying beneath the surface.
The realism and texture of the world.
The symbolism, themes, and possibilities.

text: When planning a trip, you prefer to know:

options.text: Where you will be, how you will get there, and what is available.
What kind of experience you want and then improvise the details.
Practical facts that make the trip run smoothly.
The possibilities and unusual places you might discover.

text: When someone describes a future they want, you naturally ask:

options.text: What exactly would that look like day to day?
What could that future become?
What practical steps would make it possible?
What larger idea or possibility is behind it?

text: You are more likely to trust a new idea when:

options.text: It has evidence behind it.
It connects with a pattern I have noticed.
It has already worked in a similar situation.
It opens a possibility that conventional evidence has not captured yet.

text: When faced with a familiar task, you usually:

options.text: Use the method that reliably works.
Wonder whether there is a fundamentally different way.
Pay attention to the known sequence and details.
Look for a way to reinterpret or improve the task.

text: Which kind of conversation holds your attention longer?

options.text: What happened, what is happening, and what needs to happen next.
What it all might mean.
Specific experiences and useful information.
Ideas, theories, and what might happen.

text: When making a difficult decision, what carries more weight?

options.text: Whether the reasoning is internally consistent.
How the decision will affect the people involved.
Whether the principles hold up even when emotions change.
Whether the outcome respects what matters to the people closest to me.

text: A friend asks for your honest opinion about something they created. You are more likely to:

options.text: Tell them exactly what is not working.
Start with what I appreciate so the criticism can be heard.
Focus on the quality of the result.
Think carefully about how the feedback will affect them.

text: When two people argue, you instinctively look for:

options.text: The strongest evidence.
The underlying feelings and needs.
The point at which the reasoning breaks down.
The point at which the relationship is being damaged.

text: If a rule seems inefficient, your first question is:

options.text: Why should we keep a rule that does not work?
Who is affected if we change it?
Can the rule be redesigned logically?
What would preserve fairness and trust if it changes?

text: When someone makes a decision you disagree with, you are more likely to ask:

options.text: Does their reasoning actually support the conclusion?
What circumstances led them to that choice?
What evidence are they relying on?
What values or people are they trying to protect?

text: What makes an apology convincing to you?

options.text: Acknowledging exactly what was wrong.
Showing genuine understanding of the hurt caused.
Taking responsibility for the specific action.
Showing that the relationship matters enough to change behavior.

text: When giving advice, you naturally emphasize:

options.text: What is most rational and effective.
What will preserve the person's sense of self.
The consequences of each option.
What aligns with the person's values and relationships.

text: You discover that a decision produced a good outcome for the wrong reasons. You tend to:

options.text: Still question the reasoning.
Care that the outcome helped people.
Separate the quality of the reasoning from the outcome.
Consider whether the good result changes how the decision should be judged.

text: Which criticism would bother you more?

options.text: 'Your reasoning does not hold together.'
'You did not consider how this affected people.'
'Your conclusion is based on weak evidence.'
'You made people feel disregarded.'

text: When you must choose between being precise and being kind in a difficult conversation, you tend to:

options.text: Say what is true as clearly as possible.
Find a way to preserve the person's dignity.
Prioritize accuracy first, then repair the relationship.
Prioritize the relationship while still being honest.

text: A project begins without clear direction. You feel most comfortable when you can:

options.text: Define the objective, roles, and timeline.
Keep the direction flexible while learning more.
Set milestones and make decisions early.
Leave room for unexpected opportunities and changes.

text: Your ideal weekend is more likely to be:

options.text: Planned enough that I know what I am doing.
Open enough that I can decide as I go.
A sequence of things I have chosen in advance.
A blank space where something unexpected can happen.

text: When a deadline is weeks away, you tend to:

options.text: Finish early so it stops occupying mental space.
Work best when the deadline becomes real.
Create a plan and follow it.
Keep options open until I know the best approach.

text: If plans change at the last minute, you usually:

options.text: Feel disrupted, then reorganize quickly.
Adapt easily if the new option is interesting.
Want to know the new plan as soon as possible.
See the change as potentially better than the original.

text: Which feels more uncomfortable?

options.text: Leaving an important decision unresolved.
Having a decision made before all options are explored.
Not knowing what the plan is.
Being locked into a plan that no longer fits.

text: When organizing your surroundings, you prefer:

options.text: Everything having a defined place.
Things being accessible even if not perfectly arranged.
A visible system that keeps life predictable.
Freedom to change the arrangement as needs change.

text: When someone says, 'Let's just see what happens,' your reaction is more likely:

options.text: I want at least a basic plan.
That sounds freeing.
I want to know what we are committing to.
That gives us room to respond intelligently.

text: When you have several important tasks, you naturally:

options.text: Prioritize them and work through the list.
Move between them depending on energy and interest.
Create a sequence and close things one by one.
Keep several active until the best direction becomes clear.

text: How do you relate to unfinished decisions?

options.text: They stay in my mind until I resolve them.
I can leave them open while I gather information.
I prefer closure even if the decision is difficult.
I dislike closing options prematurely.

text: When preparing for an important event, you are more likely to:

options.text: Plan the details so nothing is left to chance.
Prepare the essentials and improvise the rest.
Feel calmer once everything is organized.
Enjoy discovering what happens beyond the plan.

text: You inherit a responsibility with no instructions. Your first move is:

options.text: Establish a structure and decide what must be done.
Explore the situation before committing to a structure.
Set an outcome and organize the work around it.
Gather possibilities and see which direction develops.

text: When a conversation unexpectedly becomes deep, you usually:

options.text: Become more engaged because there is something real to explore.
Need time afterward to process what was said.
Enjoy the exchange and think through it with the other person.
Listen deeply but keep much of the experience inside.

text: When you meet someone who thinks very differently from you, what interests you first?

options.text: How they see the world and what we could discuss.
What their perspective reveals about my own thinking.
The energy of the interaction and what we might do together.
The internal logic of their worldview.

text: When you are overwhelmed, you are most likely to seek:

options.text: A trusted person who helps me reconnect with the outside world.
Solitude so I can regain internal clarity.
Activity or movement that changes my state.
Quiet reflection without needing to explain myself.

text: Which sounds more like your natural thought process?

options.text: I understand what I think by hearing myself talk.
I understand what I think after I have reflected.
Ideas become clearer as I exchange them.
Ideas become clearer when I am alone with them.

text: When entering an unfamiliar social setting, you tend to:

options.text: Make contact first and figure out the atmosphere through interaction.
Observe first and decide where I fit.
Use conversation to discover what the setting is like.
Wait until I understand the environment before participating.

text: When looking at a photograph from years ago, your mind is more likely to:

options.text: Notice what was physically there and what happened.
Wonder what the moment represents now.
Recall concrete details about the occasion.
Connect the image to a larger story about my life.

text: Someone tells you they have a strange feeling about a situation but no evidence. You tend to:

options.text: Ask what observable facts led them there.
Take the feeling seriously as a possible signal.
Wait for something concrete before deciding.
Wonder what pattern they may have sensed.

text: When designing something, you are more drawn to:

options.text: Making it functional, clear, and dependable.
Making it expressive of an idea or concept.
Using proven materials and methods well.
Experimenting with what it could become.

text: When you encounter a surprising coincidence, you are more likely to:

options.text: Treat it as an interesting event unless there is evidence for more.
Wonder whether it reveals a meaningful pattern.
Look for the factual explanation first.
Explore the possible significance even without proof.

text: Which question naturally pulls you in?

options.text: 'What exactly happened?'
'Why might this be happening beneath the surface?'
'What can we verify?'
'What could this become?'

text: A close friend is making a life change you think is risky. You are more likely to:

options.text: Point out the concrete risks and practical consequences.
Ask what the change means to them.
Help them examine the evidence and prepare.
Ask what future they are trying to create.

text: You have to deliver bad news. You focus first on:

options.text: Being accurate and unambiguous.
Choosing words that allow the person to absorb it.
Making sure the facts cannot be misunderstood.
Making sure the person does not feel abandoned by the message.

text: A team is divided between what is efficient and what feels fair. Your first instinct is to:

options.text: Define the objective and compare the costs and benefits.
Ask what fairness means to the people involved.
Determine which option best satisfies the stated goal.
Find a solution people can live with even if it is not maximally efficient.

text: When you discover that someone you care about is wrong, you are more likely to:

options.text: Tell them because accuracy matters.
Choose the moment carefully because the relationship matters.
Explain the evidence and let them decide.
Consider whether correcting them now would actually help.

text: Which compliment feels more meaningful?

options.text: 'You think clearly.'
'You make people feel understood.'
'You solve difficult problems.'
'People feel safe being themselves with you.'

text: If a tradition no longer makes sense, you tend to:

options.text: Question it and replace it if necessary.
Consider what the tradition means to people before changing it.
Test whether the original purpose still has value.
Preserve the meaning while changing the form.

text: When a plan is nearly complete, you are more likely to:

options.text: Lock it down and make sure everything is ready.
Keep it open in case something important appears.
Close remaining decisions so I can move forward.
Stay receptive until the last reasonable moment.

text: You are given two free weeks with no obligations. You would rather:

options.text: Know roughly how the time will be used.
Decide day by day.
Set a few goals and build the time around them.
See what opportunities appear.

text: When buying something expensive, you prefer to:

options.text: Research, compare, decide, and finish the purchase.
Keep looking until I feel the right option has emerged.
Create clear criteria and choose the best match.
Avoid committing until I have explored enough alternatives.
